qs.q: What is the primary definition of congenital hydrocephalus?
o: Abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid within the ventricles
Congenital malformation limited solely to the cerebral cortex
Obstruction of blood flow exclusively within the venous sinuses
Infection of the meninges caused by bacterial or viral agents
qs.e: Congenital hydrocephalus is characterized by an abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid within the brain's ventricles. It is not an infection of the meninges, which describes meningitis rather than hydrocephalus.
qs.s: Congenital Hydrocephalus: Prenatal Diagnosis and Surgical: MCQs

qs.q: An amniocentesis is performed in the workup of congenital hydrocephalus primarily to achieve which of the following?
o: Measure intracranial pressure directly in ventricles
Detect chromosomal abnormalities or genetic disorders
Cauterize the choroid plexus to reduce production
Divert excess cerebrospinal fluid from the brain
qs.e: Amniocentesis involves sampling amniotic fluid to detect chromosomal abnormalities or specific genetic disorders associated with the condition. It is an invasive diagnostic test rather than a surgical intervention to divert fluid.
qs.s: Congenital Hydrocephalus: Prenatal Diagnosis and Surgical: MCQs

qs.q: What is the primary goal of surgical intervention in congenital hydrocephalus?
o: Permanently eliminate production of cerebrospinal fluid
Repair damaged brain tissue in the cerebral cortex
Correct underlying genetic mutations in fetal genome
Divert excess fluid to prevent secondary brain injury
qs.e: The primary goal of surgery is to divert excess cerebrospinal fluid, thereby preventing secondary brain injury caused by increased intracranial pressure. Surgeries do not eliminate all fluid production or correct underlying genetic mutations.
qs.s: Congenital Hydrocephalus: Prenatal Diagnosis and Surgical: MCQs

qs.q: Which brain malformation is specifically noted as a cause of congenital hydrocephalus?
qs.e: Congenital hydrocephalus can arise from congenital malformations affecting brain development, such as aqueductal stenosis. The other options are not explicitly highlighted in the text as direct causes of hydrocephalus.

faq.a: It blocks CSF flow from the third to fourth ventricle, leading to progressive ventricular enlargement early in development.
faq.q: Why is aqueductal stenosis the most common congenital cause?

faq.a: Benign external hydrocephalus may resolve, but true congenital hydrocephalus usually requires surgical diversion.
ETV creates a permanent CSF pathway, avoiding shunt infection and mechanical failure.
faq.q: What is the advantage of endoscopic third ventriculostomy over a shunt?

exam: What bedside signs differentiate raised intracranial pressure from simple macrocephaly? — Look for bulging fontanelle, sun‑setting eyes, and irritability; simple macrocephaly lacks these signs.
A neonate with head circumference > 2 SD and ventriculomegaly on ultrasound – next step? — Arrange urgent neurosurgical referral and plan for CSF diversion; rule out infection first.
How does aqueductal stenosis appear on imaging and why does it guide treatment? — Narrowed aqueduct on MRI/CT; indicates ETV is preferred over shunt.
Why is a VP shunt still the first choice in many low‑resource hospitals? — Shunt surgery requires less specialized equipment and can be performed with basic imaging.

What infection must be screened before shunt insertion and how does it affect outcome? — TORCH infections, especially congenital CMV; untreated infection increases shunt failure and neurological damage.

Explain why phenobarbital is chosen for seizures in hydrocephalus patients in low‑resource settings. — Effective, inexpensive, minimal hepatic metabolism; avoids drugs that may worsen hepatic dysfunction common in malnutrition.
What are the red‑flag features of shunt malfunction? — New vomiting, headache, fever, abdominal pain, and rapid head growth; requires urgent imaging and possible revision.
How does prenatal folic acid supplementation reduce congenital hydrocephalus risk? — Prevents neural tube defects that can obstruct CSF pathways.
ai.title: Congenital Hydrocephalus
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Congenital hydrocephalus is excess CSF accumulation in the ventricles due to developmental obstruction or impaired absorption. It presents in infancy with head enlargement and neurological signs, requiring prompt diagnosis and surgical management.

b: Ventricular enlargement on ultrasound, CT or MRI
Head circumference > 2 SD above mean for age
sections.p: Abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid within the cerebral ventricles present at birth, diagnosed by ultrasound in pregnancy or head circumference measurement and imaging after birth.

t.b: Detects ventricular dilatation and guides timing of delivery – enlarged ventricles confirm suspicion.
Shows progressive macrocephaly – rapid rise > 2 SD suggests active hydrocephalus.
Identifies ventricle size, obstruction site – confirms diagnosis when CT/MRI unavailable.
Defines obstruction level, associated malformations – essential for surgical planning; if unavailable, rely on ultrasound.

b: Mild: FOHR < 0.4, stable head growth
Moderate: FOHR 0.4‑0.6, increasing head size, mild neuro signs
Severe: FOHR > 0.6, rapid head growth, bulging fontanelle, seizures
sections.p: Severity is graded by ventricular size and clinical impact, using the Levene or Frontal‑Occipital Horn Ratio (FOHR) on imaging.

b: Obstructive: aqueductal stenosis (most common congenital cause)
Communicating: impaired arachnoid granulation absorption
Neural tube defects (e.g., spina bifida)
Genetic syndromes (X‑linked hydrocephalus, Dandy‑Walker malformation)
Intra‑uterine infections (CMV, toxoplasmosis, rubella) – more prevalent in tropics
Maternal exposure to teratogens (e.g., certain herbal remedies)
sections.p: Causes are grouped into obstructive (non‑communicating) and communicating forms; in low‑resource settings, infections and genetic syndromes are common.

b: Macrocephaly, rapid growth on chart
Bulging anterior fontanelle, tense scalp veins
Sunsetting eyes, irritability, vomiting
Seizures, developmental delay, ataxia
sections.p: Infants present with rapidly increasing head circumference, bulging fontanelle, and signs of raised intracranial pressure; older children may have gait disturbance or cognitive delay.
Imaging defines anatomy; basic labs screen for infection and surgical fitness.

t.b: Answers: Are ventricles enlarged? Where is obstruction? – Guides need for shunt vs endoscopic third ventriculostomy.
Answers: Is there hemorrhage or malformation? – Detects obstructive lesions when ultrasound limited.
Answers: Detailed anatomy for surgical planning – Preferred if available.
Answers: Is infection present? – Treatable causes (e.g., congenital CMV) must be addressed before surgery.
Answers: Is patient fit for anesthesia? – Guides peri‑operative management.

b: Rapid head growth > 2 cm/week
Decreased consciousness, bradycardia, hypertension (Cushing triad)
Shunt infection or blockage – fever, abdominal pain, new ventriculomegaly
sections.p: Uncontrolled intracranial pressure can cause irreversible brain injury; shunt failure is a common life‑threatening complication.

b: Endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) for aqueductal stenosis – avoids shunt hardware
Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt for communicating hydrocephalus – most common in low‑resource settings
Antibiotic prophylaxis (e.g., cefazolin) before shunt insertion – prevents infection
Manage seizures with phenobarbital or levetiracetam – avoid drugs causing hepatic toxicity in malnourished children
Control vomiting and pain, maintain fluid‑electrolyte balance
sections.p: Treat underlying cause when identifiable, then relieve CSF pressure surgically; supportive care includes monitoring and infection prevention.

b: Head circumference measurement every 2‑4 weeks in infancy
Shunt check clinic: symptom review, abdominal exam, ultrasound if suspicion
Vaccination against rubella, CMV prevention, prenatal folic acid – reduce congenital causes
sections.p: Regular clinical and imaging review detects shunt malfunction early; primary prevention focuses on maternal health and infection control.

b: Benign external hydrocephalus – normal CSF flow, resolves spontaneously
Craniosynostosis – skull suture fusion, not ventricular enlargement
Meningitis – may cause secondary hydrocephalus but presents with fever and meningismus
sections.p: Conditions that also cause macrocephaly or increased intracranial pressure.

b: Normal head circumference in early weeks despite ventriculomegaly on ultrasound – do not rely solely on size
CT may miss small aqueductal stenosis; MRI is superior
sections.p: Imaging and clinical signs may be deceptive in early disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid increase in head size, bulging fontanelle, or decreasing level of consciousness
Fever, vomiting, or new neurological deficit in a child with a shunt
